newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Russian PGM supplies seen lower in future.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russian PGM supplies seen lower in future.

text.p: Russian exports of platinum group metals (PGMs) to Japan resumed last week after a six month suspension, but reduced Russian supplies in the foreseeable future, will likely keep prices higher than in recent years, analysts said.

"The key long term question is how much platinum and palladium can Russia supply to the world market, and if there is a shortfall compared with levels supplied in previous years, can metal from other sources provide an offset?," Prudential Securities analyst Clarence Morrison said.
Russia supplies about 20 percent of the world's platinum and 60 percent of its palladium.
The white metals are used in automobile emissions systems to control pollution, in semiconductors used in computer manufacturing, and in jewellry and dentistry applications.

But this year a Moscow power struggle over which government agency would control metal exports, and a change of marketing strategy, led to the suspension of platinum group metals (PGM) exports for six months.

As a result platinum prices surged to a seven year high at $500 an ounce in June, while palladium prices jumped to a 17 year high at $240.00 an ounce, before retreating to lower levels in recent weeks, ahead of the resumption of Russian supplies last week.
RUSSIAN PGM EXPORT QUOTAS SEEN LOWER

Russian export quotas for PGMs are officially a state secret, but New York based industry analysts, CPM Group, estimates Russian platinum exports will fall to around 750,000 ounces in 1997, a decline of at least 25 percent from about one million ounces in 1996, while palladium exports are expected to fall 24 percent to around 3.00 million ounces from 3.95 million last year.
Such a fall in Russian supplies would leave the world's platinum market in a supply/demand deficit of about 326,000 ounces in 1997, the first deficit in 12 years, CPM Group said.

South Africa's Anglo American Platinum Corp Ltd (Amplats), the world's largest platinum producer, said in late June it expected Russian supplies of platinum would drop by 42.6 percent, from around 1.22 million ounces in 1996, to around 700,000 ounces in 1997, and would then stabilize at the new lower level, bringing sales back into line with Russian production.

Amplats managing director, Barry Davison, said South African producers would try to increase platinum supplies in 1997 by about 9.5 percent (or about 300,000 ounces) to 3.64 million ounces to help fill the supply gap.

But one hedge fund manager, based in Russia, with access to information from the Russian parliament, the Duma, believes the 1997 Russian export quotas for PGMs may be only 200,000 ounces of platinum and two million ounces of palladium.
In June, Vladimir Rybkin, the director of Gokhran, the precious metals division of Russia's Finance Ministry confirmed Russia's PGM exports in 1997 would be lower than last year.

Several reasons have been advanced for a reduction in Russian PGM supplies in the foreseeable future: (1) an ongoing power struggle in Moscow over which government agency should control the metal trade; (2) a rundown in Russian stockpiles of PGMs, and declining production at the Norilsk mining complex where most of Russia's PGMs are produced; and (3) a resulting change of marketing strategy.
MOSCOW POWER STRUGGLE
Bureaucratic changes in Moscow look to be the main culprit responsible for the 1997 export suspension, if not for lower supplies next year.

In August 1996, a Russian presidential decree abolished Roskomdragmet, the Committee for Precious Metals and Stones, which had been responsible for Russian sales of precious metals from 1991 to August 1996.

In November 1996, responsibility for precious metal sales was given to Gokhran, a newly created department in the Ministry of Finance, while oversight of precious metal production was given to the Industry Ministry.
But in March 1997, the Ministry of Industry was abolished and absorbed by the Ministry of Economics.

Complicating the picture, Russia's central bank, already responsible for managing Russia's gold and currency reserves, also sought a role in PGM management, while Norilsk Nikel, the mining combine which produces most of Russia's PGMs, sought a greater share of the revenue from the metal it produces and sells to the state.

Currently Norilsk sells directly to the state at fixed prices, with Gokhran holding the state strategic metal reserve, and the central bank acting as an intermediary and using Almazjuvelriexport (Almaz) as its selling agent.
Almaz itself must obtain PGM export licenses from a further agency, the Ministry of Foreign Trade.
RUSSIAN STOCKPILES RUNDOWN, MINE OUTPUT UNCERTAIN
But behind the bureaucratic manoeuvering lies the hard reality of economic fundamentals, analysts said.

Last year the need for hard currency forced Russia to export much more platinum and palladium than it mines, drawing down stockpiles sharply, and pushing platinum prices down to a three year low around $347.00 an ounce, and palladium prices to a three year low around 114.00 an ounce.

According to refiner, Johnson Matthey in 1996 Russia supplied 1.22 million ounces or 24.9 percent of the world's platinum supply of 4.90 million ounce total, and also supplied 4.60 million ounces or 67.4 percent of the 6.82 million ounce palladium suppply.

CPM Group estimates Russia exported about one million ounces of platinum last year, compared with mine production of 893,000 ounces, and believes Russia's platinum stockpile could have fallen to about 0.5-1.0 million ounces.

Meanwhile, CPM Group estimates Russia exported about 3.95 million ounces of palladium last year, compared with mine output of only 2.5 million ounces, leaving its stockpile at only about 1.5 to 2.0 million ounces, though other analysts put higher estimates on the Russian inventories.

"We believe there is a distinct possibility that much of this (Russia's) above ground supply has been depleted and that the world now has to rely increasingly on mine production, which for Russia may decline in 1997," Prudential's Morrison said.
Meanwhile, in June Norilsk reported PGM production at its flagship metals plant, the Norilsky Gorno-Metallurgichesky Kombinat, rose by 3.5 percent in 1996, but fell by 26.7 percent at AO Severonikel.

But Norilsk is only producing about 70 percent of the PGMs it did in 1989-1990, analysts said, and the company continues to suffer from serious financial problems, after it warned in May of possible insolvency later this year.
The only other major source of PGM production is South Africa, which sold about 60.0 percent of the world's platinum and 25 percent of the world's palladium in 1996.
CHANGE OF RUSSIAN MARKETING STRATEGY
But a change of marketing strategy may also lie behind the reduction in PGM supplies, analysts said.

In April this year, Russia's Finance Minister Anatoly Chubais called for a new approach to raising revenue from precious metals, and Russian officials have since indicated their marketing strategy may now take more account of world prices than of bureaucratic export quotas.
"There is a difference this year - we have an amount that we may sell, not that we are required to sell," Almaz deputy director, Sergei Gorny, told Reuters this week.
Gorny explained that Almaz could now sell less than the quotas set by the government, but could not exceed the quota limits.
CONSUMERS MAY CHANGE INVENTORY POLICIES:
But a change in manufacturers inventory management policies may also provide support for PGM prices in the future, analysts said.
Until early 1997, about 50 percent of manufacturers used the forward market to lease their metal supplies, as borrowing rates were cheaper than the cost of capital.
But the suspension of Russian supplies saw world PGM inventories tumble this year, driving up lease rates to 50-100 percent per annum.
As a result many manufacturers are likely to want a higher level of PGM inventories to hedge against future supply interruptions, analysts said.

"Many of them (automobile manufacturers) have clearly put themselves in the hands of Russian stocks and the events recent months have I think quite clearly demonstrated to these companies the dangers of doing that," Amplats' Davison said last month.
